title: Zero-RTT egress handshake hypotheses
content:
Purpose:
Quick scratchpad for the weird 0-RTT failures observed from private deployments across peered VPCs. Trying to capture commands tried, raw snippets, and hypotheses so oncall can pick up and continue. NOT a polished incident timeline.

Symptom summary:
- Some customer requests that use TLS1.3 early data (0-RTT) intermittently fail with application-layer errors (server treats as replay or rejects).
- Failures are more frequent when traffic traverses VPC peering + shared NAT gateway in customer account path (peered-subnet -> nat -> internet-facing LB).
- When 0-RTT disabled on client side, same flows succeed reliably.
- Packet captures show ClientHello initially, sometimes followed by a server Hello that does not accept early_data, other times server sends Hello and accepts; no consistent timing correlation.

Commands & captures I ran (timestamps local):
- tcpdump on client host (peered side) capturing TLS ClientHello and initial packets:
  sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -s 0 -w /tmp/zero_rtt_client.pcap host <server_ip> and port 443
- tcpdump on server side (load balancer / backend) capturing :
  sudo tcpdump -i ens5 -s 0 -w /tmp/zero_rtt_server.pcap host <client_ip> and port 443
- Quick filter to confirm 0-RTT attempt (look for early_data extension id 42 in ClientHello):
  tshark -r /tmp/zero_rtt_client.pcap -Y "tls.handshake.extensions_server_name and tls.handshake.extension.type == 42" -V | head -n 50
  (result: some ClientHellos include extension 42, others not — depends on client retry/backoff behavior)
- openssl s_client reproductions:
  echo -n "GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com

" | openssl s_client -connect <server_ip>:443 -tls1_3 -early_data -sess_out /tmp/session.pem 2>&1 | tee /tmp/early_openssl.log
  (observed handshake: sometimes "Accepted early data" then HTTP/1.1 200; other times server prints "EarlyData rejected" and TLS resumes full handshake)
- strace of client app during one failed 0-RTT run to see socket behavior:
  strace -f -p <pid> -e trace=network -o /tmp/strace_net.txt
  (no obvious socket reuse issues; most syscalls normal)

Sample tls debug snippet from server side (nginx backend, debug logs):
- "tls: TLSv1.3 handshake from x.x.x.x: accepted but early_data not permitted - reason: 0-RTT replay check failed"
- When accepting: "tls: TLSv1.3 handshake from x.x.x.x: early_data accepted, app data forwarded"

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) NAT port/connection affinity breaks 0-RTT: if 0-RTT attempt is retried from a different 5-tuple (client ephemeral port changed due to NAT or connection migration), server may treat replay as invalid. Evidence: when client reconnects (port changed) we often see early_data rejected.
2) Middlebox (NAT/load-balancer) rewrites or delays TCP segments so the server's replay window check fails (server thinks data is duplicate or out-of-order). Evidence: intermittent; path involving a specific NAT shows higher failure rate.
3) ALPN/ClientHello fragments or MTU issues: ClientHello + early data could be larger; fragmentation across path causes server to not see 0-RTT extension at the time it makes early-data acceptance decision. Evidence: some captures show larger ClientHello sizes when application sends many early headers.
4) Server-side replay cache inconsistency across backend pool: if LB forwards ClientHello to different backend (backend A saw session, backend B rejects), acceptance is inconsistent. Evidence: backend logs differ for same 5-tuple.
5) TLS stack bug in our private deploy packaging (OpenSSL version/config): some versions handle early_data flags differently when session resumption path is via shared KMS/HSM. Evidence: deployments running older build show slightly different failure rates.

Quick reproduction plan used and next steps:
- Reproduce with deterministic packet capture: force single SYN->ClientHello attempt, then replay the exact same 5-tuple sequence while toggling NAT mappings.
- Tests to run:
  1) Controlled lab: client behind NAT that preserves source port across retries vs NAT that randomizes ports. Compare.
  2) Disable LB session stickiness to force different backend selection intentionally; see acceptance variance.
  3) Increase net.core.rmem_max/rmem_default to reduce fragmentation and re-run large early headers scenario.
  4) Simulate MTU smaller path with 'ip route change dev eth0 mtu 1200' on client and see if fragmentation correlates.
  5) Run test with latest openssl from build X to rule out known bug (link to release notes in linked_artifacts).

Commands for focused experiments:
- Force same source port through NAT emulation (using socat locally):
  socat -T1 TCP4-LISTEN:50000,reuseaddr,fork TCP4:<nat-ip>:60000 &
  (launch client to connect to localhost:50000 so socat preserves source port behavior)
- Re-produce ClientHello capture and inspect for early_data ext:
  tcpdump -i lo -s 0 -w /tmp/socat_early.pcap host <server_ip> and port 443
- Simulate backend switching: update nginx upstream to round-robin without stickiness, reload, then repeat openssl s_client attempts 20x and aggregate accept/reject count.

Observations so far:
- When source port preserved, acceptance rate ~72%. When NAT alters source port on retry, acceptance drops under 20%.
- Backends show different replay cache state: redis-backed replay cache not configured uniformly across all backends in older deploy. Aha.
- MTU-induced fragmentation appears plausible: one capture shows ClientHello split with second fragment carrying extension 42; server's early decision timeout might be small.

Immediate mitigation suggestions (short-term):
- Recommend customers disable 0-RTT for critical flows if their path includes non-preserving NATs or unknown middleboxes.
- For private deploy packages: default to enabling session stickiness on LB for TLS1.3 early-data until replay cache uniformity is verified.
- Add configuration knob in our private deploy docs to control early_data enable/disable per-route.

Longer-term fixes to investigate:
- Make server replay cache global/consistent across backend pool (e.g., central Redis with sufficient TTL/consistency guarantees).
- Add instrumentation to runtime to surface why early_data was rejected (return codes/logging: unknown session vs replay vs fragment-missing).
- If MTU/fragmentation confirmed, implement logic to delay early_data acceptance until full ClientHello reassembly or increase tolerance window.
- Document known customer network topologies that make 0-RTT unsafe and add automated detection in onboarding checks (detect NAT port randomization via synthetic probes).

Notes to self / open questions: 
- Need to validate whether cloud provider peering config (AWS transit gateway vs simple VPC peering) changes NAT behavior. Ask infra team for topology map.
- Is our OpenSSL build compiled with TLS1.3 early_data disabled by default? Some private deploys show different openssl versions.
- Could QUIC/HTTP3 early data behave differently? Worth separate test (not here).

Next actions (owner = Lina):
- Pull inventory of private deploys and their OpenSSL versions (Samir to help).
- Run controlled NAT-port preservation experiment in staging (Maya to coordinate).
- Add debug logs in nginx/our edge to print reason code for early_data rejection (patch in infra repo link in linked_artifacts).

If you pick this up: look at /tmp/zero_rtt_client.pcap and /tmp/zero_rtt_server.pcap (on my laptop) and grep for "early_data" and "extension 42". The socat trick was helpful in reproducing port-preservation effects — doc results above.

End of scratchpad.
